title: -s makes it plural
parentNote: Today is less a new sound than a new job for an old one: stick an s on the end and one cat becomes two cats. Say the pair out loud together — cat, cats; dog, dogs — so your child hears the ending as extra meaning, not just extra noise. Here is the thing that catches everybody out, and it is worth knowing before it happens: that s only hisses after a hard sound like t or ck (cats, rocks). After a buzzy one it turns into a /z/, so dogs is "dog-z" and pigs is "pig-z". Your child will say it that way naturally, because that is how English works; don't correct them back to a hiss. If they read "cat" and stop, cover the s with a finger, then slide it away and let them add the ending on.

activities.mouthCue: Teeth almost shut, tongue just behind them, and let the air hiss out.
activities.prompt: You know this letter already. Today it has a job: on the end of a word it means more than one.
Three quiet, breathy sounds. Find the one that hisses like a snake.
Sound out cat, then add the ending on: cat — s.

Listen hard to this ending. After a buzzy sound like g it buzzes too: dog — z.
Same buzz on the end as dogs. The letter is s and it is doing the job of a z.

One of them, or a lot of them? The ending tells you.

activities.title: Cats in the bags
activities.prompt: Read the story one line at a time. Tap any word you want to hear again.
lines: Pam did pack the big bags with hats and socks.
The cats did hop in and sat on the socks.
Pam did tip the bags and the cats ran off.
The cats sat on the hats and had a nap.
